title: 80 newborns die in 6 months at Madhya Pradesh hospital in Seoni; BJP MLA seeks probe - Moneycontrol.com
full_text:
At least 80 newborns have died in six months at the Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) of the district hospital in Madhya Pradesh’s Seoni, The Indian Express reported. Local BJP MLA Dinesh Rai Munmun has demanded an investigation and alleged that doctors are not available at night.
Hospital officials were cited as saying that about 34 deaths took place between April and June and 46 between July and September, the report said. The hospital attributes the deaths to premature births, low birth weight and complications among critically ill infants.
Rai said he carried out a surprise inspection after receiving complaints about absent doctors, demands for money from patients and a high number of infant deaths, as per the report. He claimed that outsourced staff initially tried to stop him from entering, saying a departmental inquiry was under way and an audit was being conducted. No doctor was present when he visited, he said.
Rai alleged that 46 children had died because of breathing difficulty. The hospital has a ventilator for such infants and a doctor is supposed to be assigned to it, he was quoted as saying, but the doctor does not stay at night and the nurses are not trained for the work. He also said that if the deaths were caused by doctors’ negligence, criminal action should be taken against those responsible. “Who goes to a district hospital? Poor people,” he said.
Civil Surgeon Dr Vinod Kumar Navkar said the SNCU receives critically ill newborns referred from remote rural areas of the district, the report said. Many of them are born at six, seven or eight months and need specialised care, he said. He also pointed to complications during labour and delivery.
Citing WHO and Government of India data, Navkar said a baby’s normal birth weight is 2.5 kg and that the mortality rate among premature infants weighing less can be as high as 48 per cent.
The hospital treated 1,188 newborns in the past six months, the report quoted Navkar as saying. Of these, 642, more than half, had a birth weight below normal. He said 582 infants with substantially low birth weight were treated, including babies weighing 1,100 grams, 900 grams and even 500 grams.
